title: How an Alleged Chinese Spy Got Close to Nvidia's CEO
paragraphs: On Sunday, November eighth, the boss of one of the most valuable companies on Earth sent his employees a very unusual message. Jensen Huang, the Nvidia founder famous for his leather jacket, admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife.

The next day, Nvidia's stock dropped more than four percent. And behind it all is a story that sounds like a spy movie. A businesswoman from Singapore. A secret intelligence memo. And billions of dollars in AI chips.
So what actually happened? And how much of it is proven? Let's break it down.
First, the man himself. Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in nineteen ninety-three. Today, its chips power much of the AI boom, and the company is worth more than four trillion dollars.

That means everybody wants those chips. Including China. But America limits which advanced chips can be sold there, for national security reasons. And Huang has pushed hard to sell more of them to China.
Now, meet Megaspeed. It's a data center company, set up in Singapore in twenty twenty-three. According to the New York Times, it bought around two billion dollars' worth of Nvidia hardware.
Singapore authorities have said the company is under investigation, and U.S. officials have been looking at whether those chips ended up in China. Nvidia says it found no evidence of wrongdoing.

One of Megaspeed's top executives is a woman named Alice Huang. No relation to Jensen, by the way. Same last name, different family. Photos of the two of them together at events in Taiwan have spread all over social media.

Then, in late October, the New York Times dropped a bombshell. It reported that U.S. intelligence officials had concluded Alice Huang was passing information to Beijing. And that she had built a close relationship with Jensen Huang.

Later, the Financial Times reported that an intelligence memo went further, saying the two had been romantically involved. U.S. officials reportedly believe she was recruited by China's Ministry of State Security, its main spy agency. The Times also reported that President Trump had been briefed on this, and didn't take action.

Now, here's the important part. None of this has been proven in court, and there's no public report that Alice Huang has been charged with any crime. She and Megaspeed did not respond to requests for comment.

Nvidia's first response was calm. A spokesperson said Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang were "not unusual or unexpected," because meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job. China was less calm. Its foreign ministry called the reports "baseless and purely slanderous smears."
President Trump said, "We're going to check it out very closely." And in Congress, Republican committee leaders asked Huang to come to Washington for a closed-door briefing on November eighteenth.

Then came Sunday. Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation, run by independent directors with outside lawyers. The board said it had "no reason to believe" that national security or Nvidia's secrets were compromised.

The same day, Huang sent that message to his employees. He wrote: "My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." He didn't name anyone. And he said he is committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security.
On Monday, Wall Street had its say. The Dow, the S and P five hundred, and the Nasdaq all went up. Nvidia went the other way.
Its stock fell more than four percent. For a company that big, that's well over a hundred billion dollars in value, gone in a day. Trump, though, stood by him, calling Huang "an honorable guy."

So where does all this leave us? Confirmed: Huang admitted being unfaithful, the board is investigating, and the stock took a hit. Alleged: that Alice Huang was working for Chinese intelligence, and got close to him on purpose.
Not shown publicly: any proof that secrets were actually leaked. And China denies all of it.
Next up is that closed-door briefing in Washington. And millions of investors will be watching one man in a leather jacket, very closely.
So what do you think? A real spy plot, or a story blown out of proportion? Tell us in the comments.
